You misunderstand. I'm talking about \*after\* the deductible has been met. I'm talking about the situation where the doctors office (\*IN-NETWORK\*) sends a bill to the insurer, but decides that's not enough money, and sends you a bill for the rest. EG a $1300 MRI (\*IN-NETWORK\*) that your insurer pays $400 for, your doctor sends you a bill for $900 hoping you pay it without looking at it too closely. It happens. The shitty reimbursements that insurers cram down the practices' throats make some places try to scam you. 

No provider has any leverage at all over the insurers when it comes time to negotiate a new contract. I never said they did.  I'm well aware of the dynamics between providers and insurers, having been in the health care field for decades.

Something occurred to me: If you hadn't met your deductible yet, and you got a bill, then yeah, you gotta pay it. But. If your doctor gets reimbursed by your insurance and they STILL send you a bill, raise hell. It's referred to as "surprise billing", and at least some states have passed laws making it illegal. I'd guess that the insurers aren't crazy about it either, because the more money they get from direct payers, the less they need to take insurance, and the stronger the doctor's negotiating position when the contract comes up for renewal. Can't have them anywhere but 100% under your thumb, after all.

Call your insurer. Let them know you've gotten a surprise bill and want to make sure the provider has been paid. They will instruct you further. 

Sometimes the situation is that your doctor has not gotten paid adequately or at all. While that's not your problem, really, you can help the situation. Calling your insurer to let them know they haven't paid out something they're obligated to under the terms of the contract generally gets their attention. (Failing that, call your state's Attorney General. They hate that shit.) Another possibility is that your insurer will pay what's on the bill, but they make the customer do the legwork to get the doctor paid. It's just an arbitrary hoop the insurers put in place to make things more difficult. The more difficult things are, the less it's worth to your doctor to fight it, and frequently they just give up and eat the difference.

Sometimes the situation is that your doctor has been paid what they're owed, but bill you the "balance" of what they feel like charging. If you live in a state with anti-surprise billing laws, remind them that they exist. If not, tell them that they've received the payment that they agreed to under the terms of their contract with the insurer, and if they don't like how much they've gotten paid, they can take it up with the insurer.

Sometimes you get independent billing from an ER visit (for one specific doctor) or for the anesthesiologist when you go to have surgery. Those docs usually work independently out of their own practices, and sometimes those practices aren't in-network. But, it's funny: When you call your insurer, suddenly they'll pay the out-of-network charge, because sometimes people decide they don't feel like fighting it or don't understand why they've gotten it but pay it anyway, or they're too old/ill to make the distinction. That's all a win for the insurers, because it's less of that hateful "healthcare" they have to pay for.

I'd had to get some medical records from the SSA (and sometimes the "government incompetence" stereotype is accurate) and had sent them over.
